stages.title: Reasons for wage intervention
stages.sub: Understand why governments intervene in the labour market to tackle low pay and inequality.

steps.q: A cleaner works full-time but her wage is so low that even after working every week she still cannot afford rent and food. If nobody steps in, what happens to her household?
steps.right: It stays stuck in poverty despite working
steps.wrong: It slowly saves enough to escape poverty
steps.hint: She is working full-time already. Can she just work harder to fix this?

steps.q: If a government sets a minimum wage or tops up low pay with benefits, what is it trying to fix for workers like her?
steps.right: Workers being paid too little to escape poverty
steps.wrong: Firms making too much profit from selling goods
steps.hint: Think about whose income is the problem here, and what level it is stuck at.

steps.q: A warehouse worker and a company director both work full weeks, but one earns £20,000 a year and the other earns £2,000,000. Is that gap only about how many hours each person works?
steps.right: No, it is far more than a difference in hours worked
steps.wrong: Yes, it is fully explained by hours worked
steps.hint: Both work similar hours. What else could explain such a huge difference in pay?

steps.q: If a government introduces higher taxes on top earners or stronger minimum wages to narrow that gap between the highest and lowest paid, what is it aiming for?
steps.right: A fairer, less unequal spread of pay
steps.hint: The policy targets the size of the gap between pay levels, not total output.
